H-1B BONA FIDE TERMINATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet summarizes federal requirements that apply when the H-1B employment of Jordan Lee at Acme, Inc. for the position of Software Engineer ends. It describes the Department of Labor's wage-obligation regulation, 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(7)(ii), the Department of Labor's labor-condition-application withdrawal regulation, 20 C.F.R. § 655.750(b), and the Department of Homeland Security's petition-notification, petition-revocation, and return-transportation regulations, 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(11) and § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E). It states facts about these federal requirements; it does not instruct Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee on how to respond to their particular circumstances, and it is not a substitute for the underlying Labor Condition Application, petition, or USCIS and DOL guidance.

WAGE OBLIGATION CONTINUES UNTIL A BONA FIDE TERMINATION
Department of Labor regulations state that payment of the required wage need not be made for a period of nonproductive status if there has been a bona fide termination of the H-1B employment relationship. The same regulation states that DHS regulations require the employer to notify DHS that the employment relationship has been terminated so that the petition is canceled, and require the employer to provide the employee with payment for transportation home under certain circumstances.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Payment need not be made if there has been a bona fide termination of the employment relationship. DHS regulations require the employer to notify the DHS that the employment relationship has been terminated so that the petition is canceled (8 CFR 214.2(h)(11)), and require the employer to provide the employee with payment for transportation home under certain circumstances (8 CFR 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E))."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(7)(ii) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(7)(ii) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.731)
  Known gap: The regulation itself does not define what makes a termination "bona fide" beyond cross-referencing the separate DHS notification and transportation regulations; further interpretation of the elements of a bona fide termination for wage-obligation purposes appears in agency adjudications and case law that this information sheet, limited to fetched primary regulatory text, does not address.

EMPLOYER'S DUTY TO NOTIFY USCIS OF A CHANGE IN EMPLOYMENT
Federal regulations require the petitioner to immediately notify U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services of changes in the terms and conditions of a beneficiary's employment that may affect eligibility for H classification. If the petitioner no longer employs the beneficiary, the regulation directs the petitioner to send a letter explaining the change to the director who approved the petition, rather than filing an amended petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The petitioner shall immediately notify the Service of any changes in the terms and conditions of employment of a beneficiary which may affect eligibility under section 101(a)(15)(H) of the Act and paragraph (h) of this section. An amended petition on the form prescribed by USCIS should be filed when the petitioner continues to employ the beneficiary. If the petitioner no longer employs the beneficiary, the petitioner shall send a letter explaining the change(s) to the director who approved the petition. However, H-2A and H-2B petitioners must send notification to DHS pursuant to paragraphs (h)(5)(vi) and (h)(6)(i)(F) of this section respectively."
  — 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(11)(i)(A) (eCFR text), 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(11)(i)(A) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-8/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-214/section-214.2)
  Known gap: The regulation requires notice "immediately" but does not itself set a maximum number of days, prescribe a required notification form, or designate a mailing address for the letter; H-2A and H-2B petitioners are separately directed to different notification provisions not addressed by this clause.

AUTOMATIC REVOCATION OF THE H-1B PETITION UPON NOTICE
Federal regulations provide that approval of an H-1B petition is immediately and automatically revoked upon notification from the H-1B petitioner that the beneficiary is no longer employed, without the separate notice-and-rebuttal process that applies to revocation on other grounds.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The approval of any petition is immediately and automatically revoked if the petitioner goes out of business, files a written withdrawal of the petition, or the Department of Labor revokes the labor certification upon which the petition is based. The approval of an H-1B petition is also immediately and automatically revoked upon notification from the H-1B petitioner that the beneficiary is no longer employed."
  — 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(11)(ii) (eCFR text), 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(11)(ii) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-8/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-214/section-214.2)
  Known gap: Automatic revocation under this provision depends on the petitioner actually sending notification; the regulatory text does not itself set a deadline by which that notification must reach USCIS to take effect, and this revocation rule operates independently of the separate wage-obligation and return-transportation provisions described elsewhere in this information sheet.

LIABILITY FOR RETURN TRANSPORTATION COSTS UPON DISMISSAL
Federal regulations make an H-1B employer liable for the reasonable costs of return transportation of the beneficiary abroad if the beneficiary is dismissed from employment before the end of the period of authorized admission. For purposes of this liability, "abroad" refers to the beneficiary's last place of foreign residence, and the provision applies to any employer whose offer of employment became the basis for the beneficiary obtaining or continuing H-1B status.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employer will be liable for the reasonable costs of return transportation of the alien abroad if the alien is dismissed from employment by the employer before the end of the period of authorized admission pursuant to section 214(c)(5) of the Act."
  — 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (eCFR text), 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-8/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-214/section-214.2)
  "Within the context of this paragraph, the term “abroad” refers to the alien's last place of foreign residence. This provision applies to any employer whose offer of employment became the basis for an alien obtaining or continuing H-1B status."
  — 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (eCFR text), 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-8/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-214/section-214.2)
  Known gap: The regulation's liability runs to "the alien" — the H-1B beneficiary — and its text does not extend the return-transportation obligation to the beneficiary's dependents, nor does it define "reasonable costs" by reference to a fare class, routing, or dollar figure.

VOLUNTARY RESIGNATION IS NOT A "DISMISSAL" FOR THIS PURPOSE
The same regulation states that if the beneficiary voluntarily terminates employment before the petition's validity period expires, the beneficiary has not been dismissed for purposes of the return-transportation liability provision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If the beneficiary voluntarily terminates his or her employment prior to the expiration of the validity of the petition, the alien has not been dismissed."
  — 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (eCFR text), 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-8/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-214/section-214.2)
  Known gap: The regulatory text states this distinction as a bare rule without defining what makes a resignation "voluntary" when it follows employer conduct such as a demotion, pay cut, or ultimatum; that line-drawing is not addressed by the regulation itself.

BENEFICIARY'S AVENUE TO RAISE NONCOMPLIANCE WITH USCIS
Federal regulations provide that if the beneficiary believes the employer has not complied with the return-transportation liability provision, the beneficiary is to advise the USCIS Service Center that adjudicated the petition in writing, and that the complaint will be retained in the file relating to the petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If the beneficiary believes that the employer has not complied with this provision, the beneficiary shall advise the Service Center which adjudicated the petition in writing. The complaint will be retained in the file relating to the petition."
  — 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (eCFR text), 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-8/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-214/section-214.2)
  Known gap: The regulation does not specify a response deadline for USCIS, an enforcement mechanism separate from placing the complaint in the petition file, or any private right of action created by the regulation itself for the beneficiary to collect the transportation cost directly from the employer.

WITHDRAWING THE LABOR CONDITION APPLICATION AFTER EMPLOYMENT ENDS
Department of Labor regulations permit an employer that filed a certified labor condition application to withdraw it at any time before the application's validity period expires, on the condition that no H-1B, H-1B1, or E-3 nonimmigrants remain employed at the place of employment under that LCA and that the Wage and Hour Administrator has not already commenced an investigation of the application.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employer who has filed a labor condition application which has been certified pursuant to § 655.740 of this part may withdraw such labor condition application at any time before the expiration of the validity period of the application, provided that: (i) H-1B, H-1B1, and E-3 nonimmigrants are not employed at the place of employment pursuant to the LCA; and"
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.750(b)(1) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.750(b)(1) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.750)
  Known gap: Withdrawal under this provision is only available once no covered nonimmigrants remain employed under the LCA at that place of employment — the regulatory text does not make LCA withdrawal a mechanism for ending wage obligations to an H-1B employee who is still working there.

WAGE OBLIGATION PERSISTS NOTWITHSTANDING LCA WITHDRAWAL
The same regulations state that an employer must comply with the required-wage-rate and prevailing-working-conditions statements of its labor condition application even after the LCA has been withdrawn, for as long as H-1B nonimmigrants remain employed under that application, unless the application has been superseded by a subsequently certified application.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employer shall comply with the “required wage rate” and “prevailing working conditions” statements of its labor condition application required under §§ 655.731 and 655.732 of this part, respectively, even if such application is withdrawn, at any time H-1B nonimmigrants are employed pursuant to the application, unless the application is superseded by a subsequent application which is certified by ETA."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.750(b)(3) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.750(b)(3) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.750)
  Known gap: This wage-continuation rule is stated in terms of the LCA's withdrawal, a Department of Labor filing distinct from the DHS petition described elsewhere in this information sheet; withdrawing the LCA and notifying USCIS of a bona fide termination of the petition are separate procedural steps governed by separate regulations.

RECORDKEEPING AND FURTHER INFORMATION
This information sheet reflects the DHS petition-notification, petition-revocation, and return-transportation regulations at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) and § 214.2(h)(11), and the DOL wage and labor-condition-application-withdrawal regulations at 20 C.F.R. §§ 655.731(c)(7)(ii) and 655.750(b), as of September 6, 2026. It does not address state law, the separate rules that apply to H-1B-dependent or willful-violator employers, related nonimmigrant categories such as H-1B1 or E-3, or the agency and judicial decisions that further interpret what constitutes a bona fide termination.
